title: Rob Citrone and Karen Karniol-Tambour at Sohn 2025

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Rob Citrone and Karen Karniol-Tambour at Sohn 2025.docx

speakers: Karen Karniol-Tambour (macro investor, Bridgewater; inferred from content)
summary:
Sohn 2025 panel (May 2025) with two global macro investors on the shift from the globalisation/US-centric paradigm to 'modern mercantilism'.
Conclusions: markets have barely priced the new paradigm; diversify geographically and across asset types; favour non-US fixed income, short the dollar vs euro/yen, EM (Latin America) rates and currencies, oil and gold; US rates higher near-term with a 2026 fiscal boost.

coverage.note: old vs new paradigm (modern mercantilism); investors long US
US exceptionalism; Latin America opportunity; capital staying home; diversification anecdote
market-cap concentration; slowdown and inflation; US rates view; non-US fixed income
tariff inflation vs deflation abroad; term premium; fixed income and FX positions
risk outside US; EM positions; China-only multi-asset; credit
fixed income capability degraded by private credit; oil, gold, AMX
nothing actionable beyond zero-correlated opportunities; closing banter

completeness_estimate: 0.78 - first reader caught the main macro theses (modern mercantilism, geographic diversification, non-US bonds, dollar shorts, EM, oil/gold, America Movil); missed regional-bloc and management-first method, US-yield spillover, China valuation/stimulus scenario, sovereign credit, bond-as-recession-hedge role, and mixed up speakers on two items.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: a paradigm of massive globalization, integration around the world. The US is a security umbrella to everything.
claims.claim: The last 15 years rested on globalisation, US security umbrella and deflationary easy money, making a plain S&P 500 the best asset; investment returns over decades are driven by such secular paradigms.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: we've called the new environment modern mercantalism meant to describe kind of a worldview that the state's job is to really maximize that country's its national wealth
claims.claim: The new regime, modern mercantilism, treats trade deficits as wealth transfers, pursues self-sufficiency and treats allies coercively, implying a different environment for assets.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: Markets have barely started pricing in.
claims.claim: The new paradigm is only starting to be priced, with prices still assuming the old one, so tariff headlines will be noisy but the change is fundamental.

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: global investors are so long corporate America in every kind of asset you can think of
claims.claim: Global investors are overweight US corporate assets in every asset class; a shift in allocation away from the US is in early stages and will take a while, complicating dollar and asset price views.

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: still think we have a massive edge in technology.
claims.claim: US private-sector exceptionalism (technology, financial services, capital markets) persists, so money leaving the US will not be easy.

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: we're seeing now that big change in Latin America where management is changing
claims.claim: Latin America, left for dead for 25 years, has political shifts (Argentina's Milei, elections in Peru, Colombia, Chile, Brazil) bringing better policies, with returns across equities, currencies, credit and high rates.
claims.direction: long Latin American equities, currencies, credit and rates

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the flip side of a massive trade deficit is a huge amount of current account inflows
claims.claim: US reliance on current account inflows, mostly from allies, means reduced foreign appetite for US assets cannot unwind in a day; policy of self-sufficiency pushes capital to stay at home (Germany defence example).

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: It fell by two Mexicos
claims.claim: After DeepSeek, Nvidia's market cap fell by roughly two Mexicos in a day, showing how under-capitalised markets like Mexico and Brazil are in world indices and the case for taking geographic diversification seriously.

correction.issue: Speaker likely Citrone, not Karniol-Tambour: the story starts with 'I have to tell you a funny story about that', interrupting Karniol-Tambour's sentence about the negligible market cap of Brazil and Mexico, and the Latin American market-cap point fits Citrone.
correction.fix: Citrone (probably) notes that after DeepSeek, Nvidia's market cap fell by about two Mexicos on one Monday, showing how tiny Mexico and Brazil are in market-cap terms (the case for geographic diversification, which Karniol-Tambour then endorses).

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: extremely vulnerable to a world where the US doesn't just keep beating everyone
claims.claim: Market-cap-guided investors are concentrated in the US; true diversification means markets with different growth, inflation, monetary policy and elections (Latin America, Asia).

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: I think there's very clearly some degree of economic slowdown ahead of us and some inflation ahead of us because of the set of policies.
claims.claim: Policies imply some slowdown and some inflation in the US; most portfolios are not prepared and have shrinking liquid allocations to respond or take advantage of pricing opportunities.

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: I think rates in the US are going to back up particularly in the in the 10-year sector and I'm kind of thinking that we're going to hit five to five and a quarter this year
claims.claim: US 10-year yield rises to 5-5.25% in 2025 with no Fed cuts and then a 2026 boom from tax cuts and reshoring once tariff uncertainty fades.
claims.direction: short US 10-year; US economy picks up in H2 2025 and 2026

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: 25 is where you get the pain from the tariffs. 26 is where you can actually get the fiscal stimulation
claims.claim: Tariff pain is expected in 2025 and fiscal stimulation and reshoring in 2026; faster resolution of uncertainty speeds reshoring.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: I like fixed income a lot more in other countries in the United States
claims.claim: Prefer non-US government bonds because other central banks can ease more straightforwardly while the Fed faces an inflation impulse from tariffs.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: If you're in other countries, it's much more deflationary, right?
claims.claim: Tariff effects are inflationary in the US (more so if supply constraints) but deflationary abroad (weaker currencies, lower energy), so the Fed cannot ease easily while other central banks can, and little non-US easing is priced.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: you kind of started this environment with nothing really looking like a big risk premium on treasuries
claims.claim: Part of the Treasury yield backup is investors demanding a risk premium that was close to nil when the episode began.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: in some of these fixed income markets it's like a once every 101 15 year type size
claims.claim: A systematic measure of pressure relative to history shows non-US fixed income and big currency crosses (euro, yen) at once-in-10-to-15-year extremes, which supports positions.
claims.direction: long non-US government bonds; long euro and yen vs USD

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: lots of the big currency drivers don't work that way. They're going to take a while to work through governance.
claims.claim: The dollar fall so far reflects speculative and fast money; slow drivers such as official and institutional flows move gradually, so shorting the dollar against euro and yen is attractive.

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: are places where rates can come down a lot
claims.claim: Short Japan and US rates (yields higher); play falling rates in Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Turkey and perhaps the UK where rates can fall hundreds to thousands of basis points.
claims.direction: long EM and UK bonds; short US and Japan bonds

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: my answer would be it's not the best time ever take risk but mostly take it outside the United States
claims.claim: How much risk and where is the key question; take moderate risk, mostly outside the United States.

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: I like currencies like a place like Nigeria and Turkey where they've had big devaluations and interest rates are incredibly high
claims.claim: Carry in devalued high-rate EM currencies (Nigeria 30%, Turkey 45%) is attractive; Citrone has about 70% of risk outside the US, half in EM; Brazil 2026 could be best market but risks from Lula and 500 bps hikes.
claims.direction: long NGN, TRY carry; Brazil, Argentina, Mexico

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: being able to also profit from the fact the economy has actually been weak, the bonds have been a good buy, that the currency have devalued
claims.claim: Expressing a country view across stocks, bonds and currencies lets one profit from China even when stocks do not do well; the China-only and ex-China funds were biggest winners in 2025.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the vast majority of investors when they go into a country, they just buy the stock market
claims.claim: Most investors express country views only through stocks; there is no reason to invest that way, and flexibility across asset classes is an advantage.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: you tend to get depending where you are in the risk spectrum something much more similar to equity-like risk
claims.claim: Fixed income capabilities were hollowed out in a zero-rate world as money moved to private credit, which carries equity-like risk rather than uncorrelated alpha.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: duration and currency are great alpha spaces that have seemed uninteresting for a while where rates were zero and are kind of coming back in a big way
claims.claim: With rates no longer zero, duration and currency selection across countries offer uncorrelated alpha again, though many mandates are limited to US Treasuries.

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: I think we can't underestimate the risks in Iran and Israel
claims.claim: Citrone bought oil at 55-58 dollars on Iran/Israel conflict risk, expecting a near-term spike.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: You're clearly looking at a world that has more inflation risk than it used to.
claims.claim: Commodities, including gold, are ignored but useful assets in a world with more inflation risk.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: everybody's long and oil I think people are short
claims.claim: Tactically prefer gold to oil: gold is crowded long after a big run, oil is crowded short and could spike.

correction.issue: Internally inconsistent and probably two speakers: Karniol-Tambour says she does not tactically buy oil and likes gold better tactically; the crowding argument (gold crowded long, oil crowded short, so oil could spike while gold underperforms) points the other way and is probably Citrone's counterpoint.
correction.fix: Karniol-Tambour tactically prefers gold over oil as part of an ignored inflation-risk commodity complex; the crowding argument that oil could spike near term while gold lags is a counterpoint (see added claim MT138-C06-X2).

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: generates 10% free cash flow yield trades at four times firm by EBT do growing at 10% buying back 7 to 10% of the stock a year
claims.claim: America Movil as single-name favourite: Latin American footprint, 10% FCF yield, about 4x EV/EBITDA, 10% growth, 7-10% buybacks, trusted controlling holder.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: There's so many zero correlated opportunity assets out there relative to how underutilize that.
claims.claim: Many uncorrelated opportunities exist outside the benchmark holdings, so portfolios should ask what diversifies what they hold.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: keep beating what you got before is even stronger
claims.claim: Starting prices already assume the old paradigm continues: unlike 2010, when prices embedded low US profitability, current prices assume US companies keep beating past results, so a shift in paradigm has more room to hurt US assets.
claims.indicator: US profitability expectations embedded in prices
claims.direction: US equities vulnerable to paradigm shift
claims.testable: partly - implied profitability expectations can be compared with 2010

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: we first thing we look at is management and how good is management and what are the policies
claims.claim: Citrone assesses countries like companies, starting with management quality and policy; the political change in Latin America (Milei in Argentina, spreading across the region) is the core of his thesis there.
claims.indicator: quality of country management and policy
claims.direction: long Latin American assets where management is improving

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: siloing now where you're going to have kind of the Americas, you're going to have the Europe and then you're going to have Asia
claims.claim: Citrone expects the world to silo into three regional blocs (Americas, Europe, Asia), which creates regional dislocations and opportunities in places such as Latin America.

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: We think you have to have shorts. We like we like the fact you have to protect your portfolio at certain points here
claims.claim: In a tricky, dislocated world a portfolio needs short positions and dynamic protection at certain points, rather than being structurally long.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: I particularly like currencies in places like Brazil and Mexico
claims.claim: Karniol-Tambour likes Brazilian and Mexican currencies as part of Latin American exposure, and sees capital staying at home as the US pushes self-sufficiency.

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: the last 48 hours or so have taken some tail risk off the table
claims.claim: The May 2025 tariff de-escalation removed the tail risk of massive factory shutdowns and empty shelves, but a slowdown and some inflation still lie ahead, which most portfolios are not prepared for.
claims.testable: no - view on a specific episode

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: an inflationary impulse from the tariffs is a one-off. It kind of goes through like a VAT tax increase and fades
claims.claim: The Fed's hope is that tariff inflation is a one-off price-level shift like a VAT rise, but if tariffs come with supply disruption it looks more like Covid, with demand intact and supply short, and persistent inflation; this uncertainty stops the Fed from easing.
claims.conditions: depends on whether tariffs create supply problems
claims.testable: partly - core inflation response after tariff shocks

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: the US is going force rates in most countries higher
claims.claim: Rising US yields push yields higher in most other countries, so Citrone is short both US and Japanese government bonds and plays falling rates only where local conditions differ (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Turkey).
claims.indicator: US Treasury yield spillover to other bond markets
claims.conditions: except high-rate EM where rates can fall

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: look, Chinese stocks are extremely cheap and you got to think about valuation and there's certainly a path where they stimulate and you get something out of the stocks, but it's not the only scenario
claims.claim: Chinese equities are very cheap and could rally on stimulus, but this is only one scenario, so Bridgewater earns in China through weak-economy exposures too (bonds, currency devaluation).
claims.direction: long Chinese stocks possible on stimulus

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: Argentina. I think you still get paid a lot for that. I think uh um Nigeria you get paid a lot.
claims.claim: Citrone's credit exposure is mainly sovereign: Argentina, Nigeria and Ecuador still pay a lot of yield, though they are specialised and need big returns to justify the risk.
claims.direction: long Argentine, Nigerian and Ecuadorian sovereign credit

claims.speaker: Karen Karniol-Tambour
claims.quote: if there's a recession at least I'll get some easing and that'll be kind of balancing out of all my risky assets
claims.claim: Institutions held fixed income as a recession hedge (central banks ease when growth falls); when rates were at zero that role seemed pointless, so money moved to private credit with equity-like risk, hollowing out bond-selection capability.
claims.indicator: bonds as recession hedge via central-bank easing
claims.conditions: fails when rates are at zero and cannot fall
claims.testable: partly - bond returns in recessions by starting rate level

claims.speaker: Rob Citrone
claims.quote: everybody's long and oil I think people are short
claims.claim: Positioning argument (speaker inferred to be Citrone, countering a gold-over-oil preference): gold has had a big run and is crowded long while oil positioning is short, so near term oil could spike while gold underperforms.
claims.direction: long oil, short-term caution on gold
